claims.text: Feedback-controlled mild oxidation at approximately 200 °C will induce a thin, disordered high-entropy spinel oxide surface layer on the alloy catalyst.
The controlled oxide layer will lower the oxidation onset temperature relative to the untreated catalyst.
The controlled oxide layer will enhance resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
The controlled oxide layer will improve long-term durability under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The proposed starting catalyst has a near-equiatomic, homogeneous multi-principal-element bulk composition.
The proposed starting catalyst has minimal pre-existing surface oxidation.
Real-time feedback control can limit oxidation to a nanometer-scale surface layer without causing bulk phase changes.
The resulting spinel oxide layer will incorporate several constituent elements from the underlying alloy.
The disordered high-entropy spinel layer will provide abundant modified surface active sites.
The oxide layer will shift the surface electronic structure and thereby lower activation barriers for CO oxidation.
The oxide layer will shift the surface electronic structure and thereby lower activation barriers for hydrocarbon oxidation.
The oxide layer will weaken the binding of deactivating H2O and NO species.
The oxide layer will shield the bulk alloy against degradation during thermal cycling.
The treated catalyst will have a lower T10 for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will lose less activity than the untreated catalyst upon exposure to H2O and NO.
The treated catalyst will undergo less performance degradation than the untreated catalyst during simulated vehicle-lifetime aging.
The untreated catalyst lacks the proposed controlled surface oxide layer.
The proposed improvements will persist during transient operation below 150 °C, exposure to H2O and NO, and long-term mileage-simulating durability tests.
Slight overgrowth of the oxide layer could negate the proposed benefits.
